title: Why Do Teachers in Some Schools Keep Getting Better for Longer? or-longer/
author: Sam Sims
summary: Sam Sims asks why teacher effectiveness growth, which typically slows after the first few years of a career, keeps accelerating for longer in some schools than others. He reviews evidence showing teachers improve more when working alongside more effective peers, that this effect extends to mentors and mentees, and that better collaborative arrangements correlate with stronger student outcomes -- but notes this research mostly captures the structural dimension of collaboration (who interacts with whom). Sims argues social capital theory adds two missing dimensions: cognitive social capital (shared language and interpretations that let teachers productively discuss practice) and relational social capital (shared norms and trust that sustain reciprocal exchange). He illustrates both using a Steplab documentary on two high-performing English schools, then previews his Nuffield-funded TIDE project, which will build the first validated measure of teacher workplace social capital and link it to value-added data via the new Teacher Education Dataset -- an attempt to move the theory from descriptive to empirically testable.
points: Sims's key move is to identify a gap in existing peer-effects research: it measures structural collaboration (who interacts with whom) but says little about why some collaboration is productive and other collaboration isn't.

Social capital theory's cognitive dimension -- shared language and interpretations for discussing teaching practice -- is what lets colleagues have insight-generating conversations rather than talking past each other.

The relational dimension (shared norms and trust) is what keeps collaborative exchanges from being short-lived or misaligned, illustrated by how Reach Feltham and Ark Soane coordinate around shared behavioral expectations.
Sims's TIDE project aims to close the empirical gap by building the first validated measure of teacher workplace social capital and linking it to actual value-added teaching outcomes.
quotes: Research shows that teachers rapidly become more effective over the first few years of their career. After that, the rate of growth tends to slow down. However, in certain schools, teachers keep getting better for longer.

Taken together, this evidence suggests an answer to our first question: some schools help teachers to keep getting better by providing the conditions in which teachers can continually learn from each other.
Putnam defines social capital as “features of social organization such as networks, norms, and social trust that facilitate coordination and cooperation for mutual benefit.
Cognitive social capital relates to shared language, interpretations and understandings. This is important because it allows teachers to productively engage with other teachers.

Social capital theory provides a better account of what is required for productive collaboration by specifying that relationships have to be underpinned by common understanding and trusting relationships.
This unique dataset will allow us to reveal the links between the three dimensions of social capital and the rate at which teachers improve across different schools and the departments within them.
